newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka media says scrap criminal defamation law.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka media says scrap criminal defamation law.

text.p: Sri Lankan media activists on Wednesday called for the country's criminal defamation law to be scrapped after a court handed a suspended jail sentence to an editor for libeling President Chandrika Kumaratunga.
"We are not for a moment saying that those who carry defamatory articles against others ought not be punished," said Seetha Ranjini, secretary of the Free Media Movement (FMM).
"But we are for trying them under the country's civil law and not under the criminal law," she told Reuters.
In most countries defamation is not considered a criminal offence.
On Tuesday, a Colombo judge handed Sinha Ratnatunga, editor of the Sunday Times, a suspended jail sentence of one year for criminal defamation of Kumaratunga.
The judge also handed down a suspended sentence of six months to Ratnatunga for violating the Press Council Law, which deals with publication of incorrect information.
Ratnatunga was found guilty of defaming Kumaratunga in an gossip column published in the newspaper in 1995. He said he would appeal against the verdict.

The case was brought against Ratnatunga after Kumaratunga complained to police that the article, which said she had sneaked through the back door of a hotel to attend a late night birthday party of a bachelor parliament deputy, was defamatory.
Kumaratunga says she never went to the party.
A statement issued by the FMM said it feared sentencing of Ratnatunga could be considered as a precedent in future cases filed against journalists for alleged criminal defamation.
"The Free Media Movement strongly urges the rescinding of the existing law on criminal defamation," it said.

A committee appointed by the government to advise on changes to laws affecting media freedom has already recommended that the criminal defamation law be rescinded, committee member Lucien Rajakarunanayake said.
"We have recommended the removal of the criminal defamation law," Rajakarunanayake said.

"We have suggested that if someone in government still needs to prosecute under the criminal defamation law, then the attorney-general should first report the matter to the high court and let the high court decide if the case can proceed," he said.

Last week, the government announced plans to scrap the Parliamentary Privileges Special Provisions Act of 1978, which made journalists answerable to parliament in cases where legislators were alleged to have been discredited by the media.
The privileges include the ability by parliament to interrogate and pass judgement on journalists and others who said or did things to damage the credibility and reputation of legislators.
Sri Lanka's ruling People's Alliance government has taken a tough stand against incorrect reporting of news.

In January, the government detained the director of a private television station for broadcasting what it said was a false news item about an attack by separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam guerrillas on an eastern army camp.
The director was charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, but the charges were later dropped.
